1872ecd647496d18.body:
View this post on the web at https://wufeimusic.substack.com/p/1316-a-thousand-charms

Good morning, afternoon, and evening, 
Thank you for being patient with me this past week. I was sick, but I’ve finally recovered :) Today’s solo guzheng improvisation was inspired by the Southern Magnolia I saw in China this summer. It was the biggest magnolia flower I had ever seen (photo above) — the blossom was larger than my palm, about the same size as a lotus flower. That’s why its Chinese name is 荷花玉兰 (lotus magnolia) or 广玉兰 (wide magnolia).
I wrote a poem for the flower:
广玉兰，翘盼舞伴，蜂情万种，红颜绽。
Southern magnolia, eagerly awaiting its dance partner — the bees, full of amorous affection — as its crimson beauty blooms.
Hope this piece brings you sweet dreams tonight.
Wu Fei 吴非

a3ecb8ec03fd2527.subject: Arthur Brooks: I Tried to Vacation Like a European. It Was a Disaster.
a3ecb8ec03fd2527.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.thefp.com/cp/210673270

As an expatriate in Barcelona during my mid-20s, I found many parts of life hard to understand—from eating supper at 11 p.m. to finding all the stores closed for three hours in the middle of every afternoon. But what baffled me the most was Spaniards’ sheer excellence at taking their vacation. Most of them abandoned any productive activity for the entire month of August, venturing off to the seaside or the mountains, and doing. . . well, nothing. And after this annual month of indolence, they returned victorious, radiating a deep peace. They were idleness grand masters, boredom virtuosos.
A very few years later, I would marry a Spaniard, learn both Spanish and Catalan, and adjust to the dietary routines and opening hours of my adopted country. But I never quite mastered the August vacation. Year after year, I tried to join with my wife either lounging on a Balearic beach or gazing at the mountains in a Pyrenean village. Inevitably, after about the first week, I wound up begging my wife to cut our monthlong vacation short—so that, for the love of God, I could do something.
Decades later, now living back in the U.S., I begrudgingly take brief annual vacations, but I assiduously avoid August trips to the Iberian vacation nothing-box. Lest you think I am weird (as she does), please note that I simply resemble most Americans, 55 percent [ https://substack.com/redirect/9165f204-b1f0-42c4-b7ec-facac5565f06?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] of whom choose not even to use all their vacation days.
What explains this transatlantic cultural difference—both in general and in my marriage specifically? And who has the vacation thing right? Naturally, in answering those questions, I will seek to offer a completely impartial judgment...

52773141538cd873.subject: Hecuba at the Edinburgh Fringe: A Story of War, Exile and Survival
52773141538cd873.body:
View this post on the web at https://peterfrankopan.substack.com/p/hecuba-at-the-edinburgh-fringe-a

I am in Scotland for a few days, with friends, trying to finish a book and enjoying one of the most beautiful parts of the world.
This morning I went to the Edinburgh fringe to watch Hecuba, a play written by William Stirling and Arwa Omaren, and produced by William and his wife Charlotte Eagar.
Global Threads with Peter Frankopan is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
It was a spell-binding performance, moving, amusing and devastating. It is one of the most powerful plays I have ever seen. I strongly recommend going to Edinburgh to watch it. If you are anywhere near ‘Auld Reekie’, clear some space in your diary before the end of the month; it is really worth it.
Rather than write about the play myself, I asked Charlotte - a highly distinguished journalist and former war correspondent to write a guest post for Global Threads.
I hope you will enjoy. 
And please, please do book tickets for Hecuba at the Gilded Balloon Teviot while they last.
“I was a queen, seated on a throne of gold / All Trojan women bowed before me,
My sons filled the city with pride / And every wind bore songs of festivals to my ear?”
Arwa Omaren intones to the gripped audience at the Edinburgh festival, the opening lines of her hit, Off-West End theatre award-nominated, show, Hecuba: Why Am I In Your Country?
Arwa weaves her own story of what it was like growing up as a Palestinian refugee in Syria - a country where Palestinians still do not have citizenship, despite having been there for the most part since they fled their homeland in 1948, in what Palestinians call the Nakba, the catastrophe – into that of Hecuba, the doomed Queen of Troy.
The music changes, the lights go down and up, and suddenly Arwa is alone, wailing for her. mother, on the Mountain of Death, abandoned by the people smugglers she paid $1500 to bring her from Syrian to Greece. She thought she was going to die.
“Mum! Mum!!!!!!!!
….Why am I calling for my poor Mum? I spent my life trying to get away from her!”
And Arwa gets the first laugh of the show. For unusually, Hecuba combines a harrowing tale of triumph over tragedy, with rich comedy.
I first met Arwa in February 2021 on zoom from the reception desk of the Harley street office where she was working. She was dressed in her dental receptionist uniform, like a sexy nurse in a Carry On Film. 
She was about 33 and had been in the UK since arriving as an asylum seeker in 2018. We were running on-line therapeutic drama workshops for refugees, part of our Trojan Women Project, a combined psycho-social support and advocacy drama project for refugees. 
Arwa, as a Palestinian Syrian professional actress and refugee, had been recommended to us to help run the workshops – which had become surprisingly popular. 
We had over 60 Syrian participants every week, based all over the Middle East and Europe, all of whom were improvising black comedy sketches inspired by war. This project was suggested by a Syrian refugee producer we’d worked with for several years - because a lot of funny stuff happens in wars, although it’s generally rather sick. We’ve worked with Arwa ever since.
Since 2022, Arwa has played Hecuba, the tragic former Queen of Troy, in our yearly Trojans: Why Am I In Your Country? series of drama workshops and performances for refugees and asylum seekers, based on Euripides’ great anti-war tragedy, the Trojan Women. 
The participants, almost all of whom have never acted before - with the exception of Arwa and a couple of Ukrainian professional performers who were also part of our permanent team for several years - work their own stories of exile and loss into Euripides’ extraordinarily powerful play, the first play written about refugees.
Arwa’s current show, Hecuba: Why Am I In Your Country? is different, because it’s a one woman show, written by Arwa and my co-producer and husband, the director William Stirling.
Arwa is one of the most remarkable people I’ve ever met. And her story has everything a British audience could possibly want – a tale of extraordinary danger and courage, and a dog, a baby, a husband and a happy ending.
Arwa grew up in Yarmouk, a Palestinian refugee camp-turned suburb of Damascus, the daughter of a successful Palestinian property developer. A professional actress, in 2011, she’d just graduated top of her class from Damascus’ leading drama school and signed a TV series contract - as she says in the play, quoting Hecuba, “I was a queen…I was going to be a STARRRR!!!” - when the war started … her burgeoning career was as shattered by Assad’s bombs, as her home town of Yarmouk.
After a year under attack in Yarmouk, she and her family fled to Lebanon. For the following year:
“I went into a deep depression. I stayed in my room.
I didn’t leave it for a year. I just sat there and smoked.”
Only to re-surface and build a film career for herself in Lebanon; she even starred in a BBC radio drama series about refugees – and then, age 30, her biological clock a-tick, she bought a golden retriever puppy: she called him Jacko: “he became the love of my life.”
Six years later, her family were kicked out of Lebanon, when the government decided to deport all Palestinian Syrian refugees. As for Yarmouk: “It was completely destroyed. Our house didn’t exist. We managed to save some furniture from the rubble.”
But that was the least of her problems. The various checkpoints had reduced what had previously been a 15 minute journey to six hours. She was nearly killed by an over-excited solder, firing over her head, but the greatest danger came when one of President Assad of Syria’s security officers started tracking her phone.
“I heard they were arresting actors, torturing them, to find out about other actors and artists who were against the regime….” So Arwa took the terrifying decision to pay a people smuggler $1500 to take her to the UK. She had to leave her family, worse still, she had to leave Jacko…
The smuggler said the journey to Turkey would take four hours… “but all smugglers are liars…” She ended up walking for five weeks through the mountains of Kurdistan, with an ever decreasing group of desperate refugees, led by their Kurdish smuggling gang… caught and sent back every time they tried to cross the Turkish border. 
She nearly died; she was abandoned on the ‘Mountain of Death,”, but then the smugglers returned for her… “Smugglers are very careful of their reputations for success! She was nearly raped, she nearly drowned, she was nearly shot, she had to swim rivers, take boats, but finally got to the UK and claimed asylum…
After 9 months, asylum was granted… she was safe. But she didn’t have Jacko… but as Arwa says, “I’d heard that British people love dogs…” so she found a charity called War Paws, who raised £3k to bring Jacko over. Arwa was re-united with the love of her life.
By now, she was working as a waitress and dental receptionist. She joined the Trojan Women project part-time as our drama workshops director…It wasn’t a TV career, but as she said in the first Trojans play she acted in with us in 2022 “I still dream that Martin Scorsese will come into the restaurant and discover me….”
Scorsese didn’t. Even worse, wheels came off Arwa’s life again: in October 2022, her landlord decided to sell the flat as he could not afford the mortgage, and she and Jacko were evicted. As Ealing council refused to rehouse her with her dog, she and Jacko found themselves sleeping on the streets. Being clever, she set up camp on Ealing Council’s door step…. So they could not ignore her.
She ended up in St. Mungo’s homeless shelter. The lowest point in her life. “War happens to everyone, but being homeless happens only to you…”
And then…. into the garden of the homeless shelter walked Jonathan, a nice Brit who had lost his job and his flat

218b6321e90c0e84.subject: 📈 Making sense of the AI capex logjam
218b6321e90c0e84.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.exponentialview.co/p/ai-capex-deployment-gap

For the research and modeling behind this analysis, see our 2026 State of the AI Economy Report [ https://substack.com/redirect/14227078-bb84-488d-af6a-1f7ea2332ead?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
Based on current guidance, the seven largest AI-infrastructure builders expect capital expenditure of $863 billion in 2026 – 88% more than last year. We estimate that roughly two-thirds, some $550 billion, will be AI-related. 
That investment does not begin affecting earnings through depreciation as soon as a project starts. While infrastructure is being built or assembled, the attributable costs are capitalized on the balance sheet as construction in progress. Depreciation begins only when the assets are ready for their intended use.
Across the four hyperscalers that disclose this balance, assets not yet in service now total $315 billion, up from $281 billion one quarter earlier. This represents both capacity still to come online and a reservoir of future depreciation that has not yet reached the income statement.
A dollar of capex spent by Meta now waits some 1.7 years before going live, a year more than in FY2024. So, for every dollar it spends today, only about a third will reach service within the year. Others have seen a similar trend, to a smaller extent.
In our modeling, we estimate that the Big Seven have spent more than $700 billion on AI capex since 2020. Of that, more than $200 billion is still in the construction queue; money allocated but not yet earning or depreciating. Just shy of 10% has been logged as an expensed asset.
The capex logjam is starting to show, with a depreciation bill that is lower than headline capex totals would suggest. We estimate the quarterly depreciation across the seven builders hit $14 billion in Q2, 2.4x a year earlier; 82% of it is on compute depreciating over five to six years. And this is only what has made it through the bottleneck. A third of the allocated spend is not yet contributing.
The quality of funding [ https://substack.com/redirect/84bdae1d-7894-4d91-92ff-dac4a7a3e283?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] paying for these buildouts has also deteriorated. In 2024, cash funded 85% of the Big Seven’s capex; it dropped to 70% in 2025, and is at two-thirds in 2026.
Capex guidance of $863 billion for 2026 exceeds the Big Seven’s combined operating cash flow for the first time. Some $282 billion – around a third – is funded by debt, equity and leases. Net new debt grew from $16 billion in 2024 to $161 billion (expected) this year.
On top of their own projects, the builders have pre-committed years of extra capacity. Among the five largest spenders – Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle – future rent totals $1 trillion. That capacity won’t ever pass through capex spend or the waiting room; it will instead arrive as fixed rent over the coming years.
Power supply and grid connections remain a gate, and the skilled labor for building and wiring has become another. Neither can scale as quickly as orders on paper. 
But none of this yet shows that the buildout will fail. The queues can clear, the capacity will arrive, and our own estimates [ https://substack.com/redirect/62c66ee1-363e-48c8-90fb-0c0357fc9393?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] show, demand for cheaper compute will likely follow too. Current capex reading is great news for anyone buying compute. A third of the buildout is about to come online – and its owners will be looking to earn with it.
For the research and modeling behind this analysis, see our 2026 State of the AI Economy Report. [ https://substack.com/redirect/14227078-bb84-488d-af6a-1f7ea2332ead?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]

65f81a64c7563f24.subject: Gérald Darmanin mis en cause par les syndicats de la police et de la magistrature
65f81a64c7563f24.body:
View this post on the web at https://alexispoulin.substack.com/p/gerald-darmanin-mis-en-cause-par

Gérald Darmanin mis en cause par les syndicats de la police et de la magistrature
Gérald Darmanin a répondu, dans un long message posté sur X, aux critiques acerbes du syndicat des commissaires de la Police nationale et du syndicat de la magistrature. Le ministre de la Justice a pris la parole au lendemain de la révélation par Le Monde du contenu d’un courrier adressé à son collègue de l’Intérieur, [ https://substack.com/redirect/6c69886f-1c8b-4b47-9f98-42cfe71076e0?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] revenant sur les défaillances dans le traitement des dossiers de violences sexuelles faites aux enfants.
Gérald Darmanin s'attelle, dans ce post sur les réseaux sociaux, à saluer l'investissement des différents corps de métiers dans ces dossiers sensibles. “Je sais le travail extrêmement difficile et courageux des enquêteurs et la crise de la filière investigation. Je sais aussi la difficulté des magistrats et des services d'enquête à travailler ensemble dans un contexte de grandes tensions où la numérisation de la justice est en retard”, écrit-il.
“On a l’impression que Gérald Darmanin” découvre “l’état des services de police et de gendarmerie”, avait critiqué la veille Justine Probst, secrétaire nationale du Syndicat de la magistrature, après avoir pris connaissance des révélations du Monde. Frédéric Lauze, commissaire général de la Police nationale et secrétaire général du Syndicat des commissaires de la Police nationale, a de son côté évoqué son “sentiment de trahison vis-à-vis de Gérald Darmanin”.
Il a regretté l’existence de ce courrier, qui est selon lui “une note de synthèse où on a interrogé les procureurs généraux, un rapport qui a tendance à dédouaner la justice”. Se disant “très méfiant” face à ces conclusions, Frédéric Lauze a ajouté qu’il aurait préféré à la place “un rapport de l’inspection des services judiciaires”.
Dans sa publication sur X, Gérald Darmanin défend aussi son bilan au ministère de l’Intérieur, où il a passé quatre ans. “Personne n’a créé autant d’effectifs aux policiers et aux gendarmes (plus de 8 000 !), donné autant de moyens, sous l’autorité du président de la République, et s’est intéressé autant à la protection des mineurs que lors de mon passage à l’Intérieur voilà deux ans”, affirme-t-il. Un constat qui ne semble pas partagé par l’Association nationale de la police judiciaire. 
Notre publication est financée uniquement par ses lecteurs. Pour recevoir les prochains contenus du Monde Moderne, devenez abonné, gratuit ou payant.
Benyamin Nétanyahou refuse le plan américain pour Gaza
Benyamin Nétanyahou invite Donald Trump à remballer son plan de paix pour Gaza. Le Premier ministre israélien a annoncé qu’Israël “rejetait” l’accord négocié par Washington en vue d’instaurer une paix durable dans l’enclave palestinienne, où un cessez-le-feu fragile est entré en vigueur en octobre 2025. Le texte portait sur la mise en œuvre de la deuxième phase de la trêve conclue entre le Hamas et Israël.
Cet accord prévoyait le désarmement du groupe islamiste, conditionné au retrait progressif des troupes israéliennes du territoire palestinien. Si le mouvement palestinien a réaffirmé être favorable à ce plan, Israël “n’effectuera aucun retrait tant que le Hamas ne sera pas véritablement désarmé”, a déclaré Benyamin Nétanyahou. De son côté, le groupe islamiste défend un désarmement progressif, plutôt qu’une reddition unilatérale de son arsenal.
Ce refus israélien marque un nouvel accroc dans la relation entre Washington et Tel-Aviv, déjà mise à mal par les nombreux désaccords entre les deux pays entrés ensemble dans le conflit contre l’Iran et ses alliés au Moyen-Orient. 
Si la décision du Premier ministre israélien est en partie motivée par des questions de politique intérieure, à l’approche d’élections nationales, elle entame la crédibilité de Donald Trump sur la scène internationale comme à domicile. 
Accord sur les bases russes toujours présentes en Syrie
La Syrie a annoncé être parvenue à un accord sur l’avenir des deux bases russes dans le pays, que Moscou avait utilisées pour soutenir le président Bachar al-Assad pendant la guerre civile. Les installations militaires de l’aéroport de Tartous et du port de Hmeimim, sur la côte méditerranéenne, seront transformées “en centres conjoints de formation dans le cadre de nouveaux arrangements préservant les intérêts mutuels”, a déclaré le ministère des Affaires étrangères syrien.
L’accord, fruit d’un an et demi de négociations, “a fixé un délai n’excédant pas trois mois pour achever le processus”. Parallèlement, les installations civiles des deux bases seront remises aux autorités de Damas. Le ministre des Affaires étrangères, Assaad al-Chaibani, a inspecté les installations et infrastructures incluses dans le protocole d’accord, qualifié d’“historique”.
La base aérienne de Hmeimim et la base navale de Tartous constituaient les seuls avant-postes militaires officiels de la Russie en dehors de l’ex-URSS. Elles sont restées opérationnelles pendant les négociations.
Le président russe Vladimir Poutine a reçu à deux reprises à Moscou son homologue syrien, Ahmad al-Chareh, depuis la chute d’Assad, réfugié en Russie et dont Damas réclame l’extradition. Plus tôt cette année, le Kremlin avait retiré ses forces de l’aéroport de Qamichli, dans la zone autonome kurde dans le nord-est de la Syrie.
Contrôles aux frontières espagnoles pour les voyageurs venant d’Italie
L'Espagne a commencé à effectuer des contrôles temporaires aux frontières, à ses ports et aéroports, pour les voyageurs en provenance d'Italie. Cette décision a été prise en réponse aux mesures similaires imposées par Rome après l'afflux de migrants à Ceuta.
Cette brouille entre deux alliés de l’Union européenne et de l’Otan intervient après que 72 000 migrants ont franchi la frontière depuis le Maroc vers le territoire espagnol de Ceuta, en Afrique du Nord, entre le 30 et le 31 juillet, lors d'un mouvement d'une ampleur sans précédent. 
Le gouvernement italien a assuré n’avoir “en aucun cas l’intention de revenir sur la décision de suspendre l’application de l’accord de Schengen aux ressortissants de pays tiers en provenance d’Espagne, au moins jusqu’au 15 août”. Le gouvernement espagnol a fustigé cette mesure, qualifiée “d’inéquitable, contraire aux intérêts de l’UE et discriminatoire pour la population espagnole”.
Le commissaire européen aux Affaires intérieures et aux Migrations a confirmé avoir été en contact avec les ministres de l’Intérieur espagnol et italien. “Tous deux ont confirmé que les contrôles aux frontières intérieures sont temporaires”, a-t-il réagi, se voulant rassurant.
Un entrepôt de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé détruit en Ukraine
Un entrepôt de l'Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) situé dans la ville de Dnipr “a été frappé et détruit”, a déclaré le directeur général de cette agence de l'ONU. “L’entrepôt humanitaire de l'OMS à Dnipro, en Ukraine, a été frappé et détruit. A ce stade, aucune victime n'est à signaler”, a annoncé sur X Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.
L'organisation recense les attaques contre les établissements de santé dans le monde, mais, conformément à ses règles, n'en attribue pas la responsabilité. Un membre du personnel de l'OMS et des chauffeurs s'étaient rendus sur le site plus tôt dans la journée. 
L’entrepôt “contenait des fournitures médicales humanitaires destinées aux établissements de santé de la ligne de front, principalement des fournitures d’urgence de l’OMS”, a encore détaillé le dirigeant de l’agence. Depuis l’invasion russe du 24 février 2022, l’OMS a ainsi recensé 3 148 attaques contre les services de santé en Ukraine. Elles ont fait 240 morts et 1 055 blessés.
“Je ne saurais le dire avec assez de force : les attaques contre les services de santé DOIVENT CESSER. Sinon, les gens sont privés de soins vitaux”, a déclaré Ted

92cd6850288b5dc7.subject: Why don’t some people respond to psychedelics? 5 Questions for psychologist Rachel Ham
92cd6850288b5dc7.body:
View this post on the web at https://themicrodose.substack.com/p/why-dont-some-people-respond-to-psychedelics

For anyone who joins a clinical trial for a mental health condition, the hope is that after the trial is over, they’ll feel better. And, that their improvement will linger past the end of the research, leading to long-lasting change.
The unfortunate truth, however, is that not all treatments will be successful for everyone, nor last forever—and psychedelic-assisted therapy is no exception to that rule. Despite showing promising outcomes in clinical trials so far, some people don’t respond to psychedelic interventions.
Rachel Ham, a doctoral candidate at Monash University in Australia, has been interviewing people in a large clinical trial [ https://substack.com/redirect/5a6651b2-521e-4991-802e-c82900c8fe05?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] on psilocybin and general anxiety disorder for her PhD project. She’s been learning about what the lived experience of being in a psychedelic trial is really like; she and her colleagues have been evaluating how people respond [ https://substack.com/redirect/2336f462-1ca0-4a43-89e4-787be7ddf59c?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] to therapeutic touch, and how they feel about having two therapists in the room [ https://substack.com/redirect/9e3d42dc-47d0-464d-b707-27932eadf3c7?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
In a forthcoming paper, she and her colleagues dedicated their attention to a group of low or non-responders: those who didn’t meet the threshold of a 50% reduction of their symptoms. It’s a small sample size, just seven people, but Ham thinks there’s important information to be gained from talking with them. “A motivation for us was feeling that we can learn just as much from the people who don’t have dramatic recoveries, as we can from those who do,” Ham said.
The Microdose talked to Ham about her research, and how studying limited responses can help future patients.
How do you define a psychedelic non-responder?
Psychedelic therapy has obviously shown a lot of promise, but we know that it doesn’t work for everyone. Non-response is normally defined as less than a 50% reduction in standard clinical symptom measures. We know that maybe around one-half to one-third of people meet that criteria.
For our study, we took a slightly different approach. We looked at people who did not meet that 50% symptom reduction, but we were also looking for people who had a more sustained, limited response across the whole course of their treatment.
The caveat here is when we’re dealing with real participant stories, we know that in psychedelic therapy, symptom reduction doesn’t necessarily capture everything that’s going on in this treatment. Sometimes there can be a whole host of other quality of life measures that actually improve substantially, so symptom reduction isn’t necessarily the whole picture.
And even though we often talk about “non-responders”, because this is a qualitative paper and it’s real participant stories, we’ve moved to calling them “limited responders” because it’s a little bit less pathologizing.
These limited responders go through the same therapy process as everybody else: preparation, dosing sessions, and integration. Do they just trip less? Or have less meaningful psychedelic trips? Or does their limited-response emerge later?
It’s seven participants, so we were not able to do statistical analysis, but we did look at a few acute experience measures. We looked at the challenging experiences questionnaire, the mystical experiences questionnaire, and the emotional breakthrough inventory. We compared, non-statistically, the averages between these limited responders and the broader sample. Broadly speaking, the scores are quite similar.
That’s an interesting finding out of this paper. It’s complex to make sense of, because a lot of these measures have been shown to correlate with improved therapeutic outcomes in the past. All that we can really take from that is perhaps these experiential factors don’t fully account for differences in outcomes.
Maybe there are some other pre- or post-session factors, like psychotherapeutic or relational support, that influence people meaningfully. A lot of mechanistic studies are working at a group level, so there are going to be trends. That’s very meaningful work and research. Our results caution against assuming that necessarily translates at the individual level.
How did people feel about being limited responders? Were they aware, and how did they respond?
Even within this sample, it is pretty heterogeneous. There can be quite a few different trajectories. We have three participants who show symptom scores that are increasing, which is to say that their anxiety is getting worse; we measured anxiety at three different times. And then we have four participants who actually do show reductions over time, but that did not meet the criteria for that 50% reduction.
Those are two possible trajectories of non-response. You also have another possible trajectory where someone, for example, shows a big improvement, but then has remission over time. Even within this study, we’re not necessarily capturing all of the different trajectories of limited response.
Something that we did as part of our qualitative analysis was utilize a framework that’s based around illness narratives, which explores different features of people’s storytelling in relation to their psychedelic experience and their treatment trajectory overall. A feature that we found within that was that there were some participants who tended to describe their trajectories in more sort of hopeful or future-oriented styles of narratives that kind of resembled a quest. There was something really hopeful and progress-oriented around those stories.
There were others, though, whose narratives were more marked by ambivalence and fragmentation and unresolved distress. That has been described as a chaos narrative.
These kinds of narratives might represent different stages of an ongoing therapeutic process, rather than stable endpoints.

Do you consider a limited response to be a kind of challenging psychedelic experience?
I would come back to the message that a limited response is quite heterogeneous. It’s not really a story about responders and non-responders. For a lot of people, healing is non-linear; it’s ongoing and it takes work, and that’s all deeply individual.
We did see some really challenging experiences. We had one participant that had a somatic re-experiencing of sexual assault. Another who had an emergence of a memory about childhood sexual abuse, alongside a sexuality related insight. Another witnessed violent imagery. We know that these challenging experiences have quite a lot of nuance, including what they mean in the context of psychedelic therapy and outcomes.
There’s some research by Max Wolff that looks at [ https://substack.com/redirect/dc22d758-c35d-4f95-9caa-081edee11775?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] the acceptance process during psychedelics, and how that influences outcomes. We can start to imagine some of these mechanisms might contribute to whether a challenging experience translates into benefit or or harm. Our findings raise questions around how particular forms of challenge might indicate potential vulnerability. By trying to understand these more complex trajectories, we can build models of care that are safer, more reflexive, and therefore more ethical and more effective.
Something that I think was quite interesting is that all participants felt that they had benefited from their psychedelic experiences. I don’t want to say that too flippantly, because for a lot of people, that feeling of benefit was also accompanied by quite considerable distress. You

Claire built an AI agent that reviews pull requests, scores their risk, auto-approves the safest ones, and sends anything questionable to Slack. In this episode, she breaks down how she built the entire thing in one Codex session using Vercel Eve, and why letting AI review AI-generated code may be a lot less risky than it sounds.
Biggest takeaways:
You don’t need a human to review every AI-generated PR. That may sound reckless, but it’s increasingly looking like the smarter operating model. Intercom has already shown this can work at scale: PRs approved by its AI system move five times as fast as human-reviewed ones and have a lower revert rate. In other words, the AI-reviewed code isn’t just shipping faster—it’s less likely to need fixing after it reaches production.
The key is having a clear way to separate changes that can skip human review from ones that can’t. The risk model used here scores each PR across six dimensions: the size of the change, its blast radius, how easily it can be reversed, its data and security implications, its operational impact, and whether tests and CI have actually been completed. Anything below 24 points is classified as low risk and cleared by the agent; anything above 64 goes straight to a human for review. The exact numbers matter less than turning a vague judgment call into a repeatable system.
Vercel’s Eve may be the fastest way to deploy a serious internal AI agent across Slack and GitHub without spending weeks building infrastructure. It handles the annoying plumbing—connectors, refresh tokens, sandboxing, and routing across channels—so the actual work becomes writing instructions and skills in Markdown instead of babysitting OAuth flows.
A useful internal agent can now be built and deployed in a single Codex session, starting with a prompt that’s only a couple of sentences long. In this case, the initial ask was essentially: build a GitHub bot that waits for checks to pass; grades each PR as low, medium, or high risk; and automatically approves the low-risk ones. Everything after that was steering and refinement, not a giant up-front specification.
Browser use removes much of the configuration tax that makes agent setup feel harder than it should. Creating a Slack bot and GitHub app manually normally means clicking through endless permission screens, choosing scopes, and managing tokens. Codex handled almost all of that through the browser. The human’s job was mostly to click “save” and complete 2FA. What usually takes hours took minutes.
SOC 2 compliance and automatically approved PRs are not inherently at odds. The important part is making the process legible: the risk model needs to be reflected in the company’s code-review and security policies, every decision needs to be logged, and the resulting audit trail needs to be easy to query and defend. The security team’s role is to help design the right framework, not simply block automation because it feels unfamiliar.
The operational design matters just as much as the underlying technology. Merge Mommy doesn’t actually merge anything. Instead, it posts a gray check in GitHub as a signal, then sends a Slack message with the risk score and a note saying the PR is ready to approve and merge. That small handoff preserves human accountability for the final action while eliminating most of the cognitive work involved in reviewing a routine change.
Evals are what keep internal agents trustworthy after the novelty wears off. Intercom logs every PR review its agent produces and then has an engineer assess whether the score and recommendation were correct. That’s the same discipline strong teams already bring to customer-facing AI products. Internal agents may feel less visible, but when they touch something as important as the codebase, they need the same protection against regressions.
The surprising thing about building an Eve agent is how little “building” is actually involved. The full instructions for Merge Mommy fit on roughly a page: a few paragraphs, a handful of bullets, and a short skill file. There isn’t much framework-specific magic to learn. The core skill is simply being able to explain, clearly and precisely, what the agent should do.

 Anime, and More

View this post on the web at https://www.statsignificant.com/p/6-culture-trends-worth-watching-netflixs-534

Welcome back to the Monday Roundup! 
The Monday Roundup is a weekly bonus edition featuring data-driven culture stories, curated datasets, and recommended reading. 
Your regular Wednesday essay stays free for everyone—this is strictly additive.
Today’s edition has six new data stories. Free readers get the first two; paid subscribers get the full thing, plus datasets and recommended reading. Enjoy!
In Today’s Roundup:
Original Data Stories: anime’s global dominance, the Netflix afterlife phenomenon, Latin music’s outsized presence on YouTube, a Dunesday box-office showdown, the WNBA’s remarkable resurgence, and ancient Greece’s return to the mainstream (following a 3,000-year hiatus). 
Recommended Reads: Notable data journalism and pop culture reads from around the web.
Unique Datasets: Ten publicly available datasets, covering everything from music genre popularity to Nobel Prize winners to IMDb data dumps.
Trend 1: Anime’s Global Domination
The seventh-highest-grossing movie of 2025 was an anime film called Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba Infinity Castle, which earned nearly $800 million worldwide. The astounding commercial success of Demon Slayer marked another mainstream moment for anime (though does something really qualify as a “moment” if that art form increasingly is the mainstream?).
This past week, Demon Slayer finally arrived on streaming, becoming available to all Crunchyroll subscribers, and quickly emerged as one of the most heavily reviewed films online.
And if that last sentence reads like absolute gibberish to you—especially the word Crunchyroll—then prepare to learn about a cultural phenomenon hiding in plain sight.
The past twenty years have seen anime embraced across the globe. Despite the industry’s commercial stagnation within Japan, the format has flourished abroad, growing from $2.5B in sales in 2009 to $14.3B in 2024.
Anime has become a pillar of global youth culture, with more than 42% of Gen Z Americans watching anime adaptations weekly.
One of the biggest drivers of this phenomenon is also its greatest beneficiary: a Sony-owned anime streaming service called Crunchyroll, which grew its subscribership from 5M in 2021 to 21M in 2026.
That’s 16 million paying subscribers added in 5 years, which is greater than the telecast audience of the Grammys, or the population of Belgium.
Trend 2: The Netflix Afterlife Phenomenon
If you check the Nielsen Top 10 charts right now, you’ll find that a 2010s cable TV series called The Last Ship is one of the most widely consumed shows on streaming.
This series had a fairly unremarkable run on cable television, debuting to mixed reviews and experiencing declining viewership with each successive season as cord-cutting customers abandoned linear television for Hulu and HBO Max.
So why is The Last Ship back in the cultural conversation? Presently, this once-obscure show is trending for two reasons:
The series boasts a full catalog of 56 episodes, each running 45 minutes.
All 56 episodes of this show were added to Netflix this past June.
The Last Ship is the latest entry in a rapidly expanding canon of dormant TV shows briefly resurrected by Netflix, joining a cohort of programs headlined by Suits, Animal Kingdom, and Dexter.
Given the continued existence of this Netflix-specific phenomenon, my hot take is this: there is a cohort of streaming subscribers who value volume above all else. These consumers have grown accustomed to binge-watching, and do not discriminate against cable TV programming or shows that predate the very existence of streaming.
If I were running an entertainment consulting business, my go-to advice would be: produce several seasons of an obscure cable television show, end that series, wait a few years, and then license it to Netflix.
Trend 3: YouTube Loves Latin Music
Two weeks ago, I launched a new dashboard to track the topics most frequently mentioned on YouTube, much akin to Google Trends. Before building the data pipeline, I made my best guess on the pop stars and movies that would top my rankings. Would Michael Jackson see the most mentions? What about Taylor Swift? Surely her music videos exist in a constant state of mass consumption.
Yet when my query finally loaded, I was left with an absolute head-scratcher...

5217b6474ebc3f0a.subject: Dutch Bros: The Anti-Starbucks
5217b6474ebc3f0a.body:
View this post on the web at https://gadallon.substack.com/p/dutch-bros-the-anti-starbucks

In May, Dutch Bros reported first-quarter revenue of $464.4 million [ https://substack.com/redirect/2e6ed571-eef2-4f85-9f89-b9d82fa576a8?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], up 30.8% from a year earlier, and raised its 2026 opening target to at least 185 new shops [ https://substack.com/redirect/6a668e75-dbe4-4b29-88c2-ed8084c9bcc9?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].  They plan to reach 2,029 shops by 2029 [ https://substack.com/redirect/4fe8ff23-af23-4888-a8c9-57568e466d79?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (Management repeats the pun at every opportunity).
Eight months earlier, Starbucks had announced a $1 billion restructuring [ https://substack.com/redirect/4e0d3d07-b690-4e35-b69e-c2f076f6c844?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], 627 store closures  [ https://substack.com/redirect/f2d22549-6655-470f-be14-e0093157ab6a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ](more  [ https://substack.com/redirect/f2d22549-6655-470f-be14-e0093157ab6a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]than 90% in North America), the elimination of 900 corporate roles, and $892 million in charges for fiscal 2025.
Two coffee companies are moving in opposite directions.
How does that happen? The lazy answer is that Gen Z likes sugar. We can do better.
The narrative on the street is that Dutch Bros wins in terms of format. A small box, one or two windows, no customer seating, and a menu of sweet, customized, caffeinated drinks targeting a younger audience.
And as usual, there is truth in that.  But, as usual, this is not sufficient, because the format is the most copyable part of the business.
7 Brew, Scooter’s, and Ziggi’s all run some version of the same box, and 7 Brew is the natural counterexample: it passed 600 locations at the end of 2025 [ https://substack.com/redirect/0d1e8d17-402e-47e5-88a6-a2690d8a00ff?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], reaching in under a decade a count that took Dutch Bros three, by expanding through multi-unit franchisees.
This article discusses a topic we do not address often enough in operations: the role of culture in scaling, specifically in scaling decision-making.
Starbucks scaled up its shops and assumed the culture would keep up.
Dutch Bros scales people and lets the shops catch up.
I will walk the comparison through my SCALE framework. Is the business Scalable? Does it understand its Constraints? Is it aligned? Is it well-led, aligned, and efficient?
S: Scalable
Let’s start with a distinction I always insist on: Growth just means more revenue (na din this case, more shops.) Scalability means margin expansion as you grow: each incremental dollar of revenue should come in a little cheaper than the one before.
Plenty of chains grow 30% a year without ever passing this test, and some of them find out too late that they were never scalable at all. Sweetgreen: I am looking to you.
In 2021, Dutch Bros generated $497.9 million in revenue. The guidance for 2026 is $2.05-$2.08 billion. Revenue more than tripled in four years.
Now look at what happened to margins over the same period: Adjusted EBITDA margin bottomed at 12.3% in 2022, commodity costs, wage inflation, and the strain of opening 133 shops in a single year, and then climbed: 16.6% in 2023, 18.0% in 2024, 18.5% in 2025. EBITDA grew 31.4% last year against revenue growth of 27.9%.
But as the graphs above indicate, the latest quarter complicates the story: Adjusted EBITDA margin in Q1 2026 slipped to 17.1% from 17.7% a year earlier, as pre-opening costs outpaced revenue.
But this is a reminder that margin expansion while growing is not a birthright; it gets re-earned every year the opening schedule accelerates.
The composition of the growth matters as much as its size. The 8.3% systemwide comp breaks down into 5.1% transaction growth and 3.2% ticket growth.
Most of that comp is traffic, not price. I usually discount price-heavy comps, since they borrow against the brand’s goodwill; this one is mostly incremental demand.
The final scalability question, which, to be frank, I hardly address, is geographic: A drive-through coffee brand built on Oregon car culture could plausibly have been a taste that dies at the Rockies. The early evidence points the other way: new markets [ https://substack.com/redirect/4fe8ff23-af23-4888-a8c9-57568e466d79?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] in  [ https://substack.com/redirect/4fe8ff23-af23-4888-a8c9-57568e466d79?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]Florida, Tennessee, and Kentucky are producing average unit volumes of roughly $1.7 million, which management says match its legacy Pacific Northwest markets at the same stage.  The footprint reached 25 states at the end of 2025, and management believes the first 18 alone could support 3,500 shops.
In other words, demand, so far, is not the binding constraint … So what is?
C: Constraints
Long-time readers know my mantra: Tell me what constrains you, and I’ll tell you where your strategy should focus.
Note what the constraint is not.
Capital?  Operating cash flow funds most of the expansion, with leases and credit facilities filling in the gaps.
Real estate? CEO Christine Barone has described approving more than 30 sites per month, a pace that would keep most real estate departments busy just printing the leases. The 10-K lists sites, leases, permits, construction, and financing as conditions for growth, and all of them are real enough.
But the constraint management deliberately chose to let people govern the system. Every new shop requires a manager and a trained crew, and for roughly every three to seven shops the company needs one more regional operator, a role it fills exclusively from within.  No external hires.   None!
Joth Ricci, the CEO who took the company public, said it directly [ https://substack.com/redirect/b1589463-28fb-41f9-ab5b-3c4797190ac8?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]: “We are not a real estate company. Our primary focus is not site availability, it is people development.”
Sumi Ghosh, his head of operations, went further: the company will not open new shops “unless, and until, we have great people to operate them.”
Executives say things like this all the time, and the numbers usually embarrass them….
Not here.
According to the fiscal 2025 10-K [ https://substack.com/redirect/28c42e92-dc75-43f0-ab22-183e3970ec96?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], Dutch Bros carries approximately 475 qualified regional operator candidates with an average tenure of over 7.5 years, and targets 100% internal promotion for the role.
In November 2021, that bench held 200 candidates. The bench more than doubled during the exact years the company was opening 130 to 160 shops annually, the pipeline grew faster than the shop count it feeds.
The 2029 plan requires roughly 900 additional shops. In January 2025 commentary [ https://substack.com/redirect/4fe8ff23-af23-4888-a8c9-57568e466d79?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], management sized the bench as sufficient for approximately 1,500.
I would not read that as proof that the entire 2029 staffing requirement is prepaid; management sizing moves around, but the sequencing is the story: The normal sequence in this industry is to lease first, manage later.  Dutch Bros inverted it, and carries leadership as inventory: a work-in-process stock of managers built years ahead of demand.
A: Aligned
Alignment, in the SCALE framework, refers to the coherence between the value proposition and the operating model.
The Dutch Bros promise is a textbook definition of focus: a heavily customized drin

40f32fd560b941a2.body:
View this post on the web at https://stephenfollows.com/p/what-percentage-of-hollywood-film

Last week I gave a keynote at the Locarno Film Festival [ https://substack.com/redirect/4eee2737-23bf-42f9-84fe-e2f2b74625d7?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ], following a request by the organisers to give the well-connected audience a ‘slap in the face’.  This is exactly the kind of brief I relish, so I covered the hard realities of profitability, gatekeepers, and nepotism.
To prepare, I gathered the biographies of the 6,921 people who wrote, directed, or starred in the 100 top-grossing films of each year since 2000 (2,600 films in total). I then looked at who had a family member already in the entertainment industry before they joined. 
I was excited to share the results, although I wasn’t quite ready for the reaction.  As the Hollywood Reporter put it  [ https://substack.com/redirect/80a336c0-6301-48d9-9cba-8ef23cc57615?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]“the surprise, or shock, of the audience was audible”. I thought it was fairly well known just how nepotistic the top of Hollywood is, but it seems that most people were not expecting the scale the data revealed.
So let’s dig into the findings.
What counts as a ‘nepo baby’?
The word ‘nepotism’ entered English in 1669 via a scandalous book called Il nepotismo di Roma, about the popes’ habit of making cardinals of their ‘nephews’ (itself just a polite word for their bastards). The insult ‘nepotism baby’ has been in print since at least 1915, when a Missouri newspaper used it to attack a state governor for stuffing the payroll with relatives. 
The earliest traceable use of its newer form, ‘nepo baby’, is a December 2020 tweet about Jack Quaid, son of Dennis Quaid and Meg Ryan, and Urban Dictionary had an entry by July 2021. In December 2022, New York Magazine put a gaggle of famous actors’ faces on babies’ bodies and declared it ‘The Year of the Nepo Baby’ [ https://substack.com/redirect/1e65e76c-849e-405b-86f5-c5ea02b6474a?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. 
While the term ‘nepo baby’ is fun and evocative, it’s a little imprecise for the data research, so instead  I am going to refer to people who have family ties within the industry. 
I counted someone as having family ties if a parent or close blood relative (i.e. a sibling, grandparent, uncle, aunt or cousin) worked in film or television before that person’s own entry into the industry. 
I excluded spouses and partners as it takes most people years to get into the industry, so a partner who works in film is far more likely to be a consequence of being in the industry than the way in. Secondly, I also excluded relatives who joined up after our subject did. There’s more detail in the Notes at the end of this article.
How commonplace is it for film folk to have family ties in the industry?
Of the people I studied, roughly a quarter had a family member already in the film or TV industry before they joined. 
Top-billed actors lead on 28%. Directors are close behind on 26%. Writers come out lower, on 18%, though they are also by far the least written-about group, so there’s a greater margin of error.
All this means that when Jamie Lee Curtis, daughter of Tony Curtis and Janet Leigh, declared herself [ https://substack.com/redirect/fb3a56cb-0215-462f-b0cd-b69f2fbccc84?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] ‘an OG Nepo Baby’ and wrote ‘I am not alone. There are many of us’, she was spot on. There are many of them - about one in four.
How many films have connected creatives?
As well as helping the individuals themselves, a film project can really benefit from having an industry veteran rooting for it.
So let’s flip from people to films. For each of the 2,600 films, I counted how many people with family ties sat in its core creative team, i.e. the director, the credited writers and the top three billed actors.
30% of top films have no nepo baby anywhere in their core team. 36% carry exactly one, 23% carry two, and 11% have three or more.
Put the other way round, seven in ten of the biggest films of the past 25 years had at least one person with industry family at the heart of their creative team. This was the headline stat that shocked the folks in Locarno.
Is it getting better?
While the term ‘nepo baby’ might be new, nepotism in Hollywood most certainly is not. Universal founder Carl Laemmle reportedly kept more than 70 relatives on the payroll [ https://substack.com/redirect/ccc71df3-464f-48fc-9572-3545fb2ea373?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] (including making his son head of production as a 21st birthday present), and the Barrymore acting dynasty [ https://substack.com/redirect/f773101d-063d-44a0-a60b-0c32e843f1e8?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] was on its third generation even before talkies arrived. 
The rate of already-connected directors has not wavered for two and a half decades. The most recent period I looked at (2020-24) saw a slight dip, but not because things improved but because the composition of ‘top-grossing movies’ changed due to the pandemic.  Bigger movies were held back, and more indie movies cracked the ‘Top 100’.
Does it help in the longer-term?
Having a leg up at the start of your career is not the same as having a career-long advantage. When you listen to actual nepo babies talk about their experience, they tend to reflect the same idea: that it’s only an advantage of breaking in. Lily-Rose Depp told Elle magazine [ https://substack.com/redirect/54adf8dc-bdc5-4b4e-8d7e-98a33480674e?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]:
Maybe you get your foot in the door, but you still just have your foot in the door. There's a lot of work that comes after that.
Gwyneth Paltrow said much the same [ https://substack.com/redirect/b1b0325e-8e9f-49f3-8a74-4ff7a640f468?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]: 
you get access other people don't have, so the playing field is not level in that way. However... once your foot is in the door, which you unfairly got in, then you almost have to work twice as hard and be twice as good.
So I tested if the data supports this idea.  And it does.
Films directed by industry-family directors have a median adjusted domestic gross of $84m, compared with $87m for films directed by everyone else. 
The films were also not any better, according to IMDb audience ratings. 
So what does a famous surname actually buy?
I narrowed in on the 1,804 directors whose debut feature since 2000 attracted a meaningful audience, whether or not their career went anywhere afterwards. 
Connected directors get their first film made younger (a median age of 33 against 35), and those who eventually reached the top 100 climbed faster (a median of 8 years from first feature against 10). 
Most of all, they get more chances. 72% went on to a second feature against 66% of everyone else, and their median career is three features against two.
Family ties get you a modest start earlier, keep you in the game longer, and buy you another roll of the dice when a film disappoints. The surname is more of a safety net than some kind of accelerator or guarantee. 
Talent, it turns out, is not hereditary. Access is.
Director Jason Reitman, son of Ivan, put it rather pithily when telling NPR [ https://substack.com/redirect/609ff750-f344-4d1a-915c-467b38c1ead4?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] about the reception of his first film:
People presumed that nepotism would pave the road for my career. And nepotism let me down, frankly.
Epilogue
The point of today’s research is not to imply that having family ties is inherently a bad thing, or that the people who benefit from them are villains. If you grow up around the industry, you absorb it. You get a cha

It’s Monday, August 10. This is The Front Page, your daily window into the world of The Free Press—and our take on the world at large. Today: The transformation of the Democratic Party. Russ Greene on the return of the suburban dream. Liz Wolfe on Montessori gone wrong. And much more.
But first: The celebrity-backed nonprofit facing scrutiny for terror ties.
For nearly 40 years, a Bay Area charity called the Middle East Children’s Alliance (MECA) has been one of the most high-profile backers of the Palestinian cause. The charity itself has also had high-profile backers, including luminaries from Hollywood, academia, and beyond.
MECA says it spends its money solely on schools, scholarships, water projects, and medicine. But were the donations it sends from progressive Americans to the Middle East in fact channeled to terror-linked groups? And is the charity partnered with groups aligned with hostile actors?
Those are the questions being investigated by Washington, and the subject of Jay Solomon’s latest report for The Free Press.
—The Editors
Two Views of the Democratic Party’s Transformation
The year 2026 is proving to be pivotal for the Democratic Party. In primary after primary, voters are picking candidates further and further to the left. Nearly a third [ https://substack.com/redirect/5fc49773-4c18-47fa-b2ef-2f9ad640016c?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] of Democrats now identify as democratic socialists, backing policies like Medicare for All, free college, and ending U.S. military aid to Israel. The party is changing fast, and today, we have two conversations to help make sense of where it’s heading.
First, Coleman Hughes sits down with Rep. Ro Khanna on the latest episode of Conversations with Coleman. Khanna hails from the party’s progressive wing and has distinguished himself as one of the Democratic Party’s loudest critics of Israel, and last month went viral after claiming he was detained by Israeli settlers and the IDF in the West Bank. Coleman presses the Silicon Valley congressman on his claim that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, his theory of progressive capitalism, and whether Democrats can actually deliver for the working class they keep promising to fight for. This is a conversation you won’t want to miss.

Two Republicans, Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski, crossed party lines to oppose Blanche over concerns about the Justice Department’s independence under his leadership.
Former president Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread [ https://substack.com/redirect/9cdb71dd-2940-4b9b-b5a3-474a23151733?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] to his bones, his son Hunter Biden revealed late Friday in an interview, saying the condition is taking a serious toll. “I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good,” Hunter said, adding that despite the “very painful” and “very debilitating” consequences of his father’s cancer, the former president remains publicly engaged and “still doing his thing.”

Italian divers discovered a 2,100-year-old Roman shipwreck [ https://substack.com/redirect/2cf42a53-b57a-4d2d-b94a-0507e61194b4?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] off the coast of Sicily, packed with hundreds of remarkably preserved clay jars. In less than three weeks, the first day of school arrives for Yorktown High School in Arlington, Virginia, which has about 2,600 students and is so academically ambitious that the 10 heaviest backpacks [ https://substack.com/redirect/e5e296fa-3b28-420b-8b7d-ffbaae502780?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] worn by students exceeded 20 pounds each, The Yorktown Sentry student newspaper reported in April. Yorktown’s mission statement says that it will “support students by name, strength, and need.”
But an investigation by the Virginia attorney general’s office into how the high school responded to complaints of antisemitism both before and after the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel concluded that Yorktown failed to live up to its words or to protect Jewish students. The findings have not been released to the public, but The Free Press exclusively reviewed a 39-page summary of evidence gathered by the Virginia attorney general’s office and its conclusions, issued in October.
One male Jewish student reported being repeatedly targeted because he wore a kippah, which a female classmate tried to pull off his head. After a male student called him an antisemitic slur, he began covering his kippah with a baseball cap. A female Jewish student said that she was chased because she was Jewish, and other Jewish students described seeing Nazi salutes, hearing Holocaust jokes, and being told that they belonged in a gas chamber or that “Hitler should have finished the job.”
In detail after detail, the document paints not only a damning and dispiriting picture of surging antisemitism but also the indifference with which the incidents were met by school officials. Even though they warned that harassment of Jewish students would not be tolerated, Yorktown’s principal and other school leadership almost never followed through with any punishment. The result was a systemic failure to rectify the overarching issue of antisemitism affecting Jewish students, according to the report. It concludes that Arlington County Public Schools (APS), which includes Yorktown, was “deliberately indifferent to a discriminatory hostile environment against Jewish students at Yorktown High School.”
Investigators in the attorney general’s Office of Civil Rights also concluded that there was “reasonable cause” to believe that APS violated state and federal antidiscrimination laws by failing to adequately respond to the hostile environment at Yorktown...

**PRODUCT HUNT — LAUNCHING SOON **🙌

The 1752vc Pitch Deck Analyzer goes live on Product Hunt soon. Get on the launch list and we'll send you the link the moment we're live — plus **5 free deck reviews** if you join the conversation on the day.

👉 _**[Count me in](https://share.hsforms.com/2qAL5cp_9RaORTQVHwr4tpwr18dy?utm_source=vc_unfiltered&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=ph_waitlist)**_

# **Will AI Eat the VC?**

Every investor I know is quietly afraid of the same thing.

Not a market crash. Not a dry LP. A piece of software that does the job better than they do.

And here's the uncomfortable part: for half the job, it already does.

85% of VC firms now run on AI — up from 76% a year ago. 82% use it for deal sourcing. Between 55% and 72% use it in diligence. EQT's _Motherbrain_ tracks more than 15 million companies and flags the promising ones an average of 14 months before they go raise. Reuben, Harmonic, Specter, Affinity — the stack is real, it's deployed, and it's cutting partner hours per inbound deal by 60 to 80%.

So let's ask the question everyone's avoiding at the LP dinners.

If a machine can source, screen, and diligence — what exactly is the VC for?

## **What AI Actually Eats First**

Be honest about what most of venture capital actually is.

It's reading decks. It's pulling LinkedIn histories. It's building the comp set. It's checking the cap table for landmines. It's writing the memo nobody reads twice. It's tracking 200 companies in a spreadsheet and pretending that's "market mapping."

That's not investing. That's administration with a Patagonia vest.

And administration is exactly what AI was built to eat.

A GP can now upload a deck into a system and watch it extract the founder, pull the metrics, score the deal against the thesis, and queue it for review — in minutes. A solo GP can operate with the leverage of a ten-person fund. The associate grind that used to justify a two-and-twenty fee? Automated by Tuesday.

Here's the reality: AI isn't coming for the venture capitalist. It's coming for the analyst. And a frightening number of "venture capitalists" are just analysts who raised a fund.

## **The Information Moat Is Already Gone**

For thirty years, the edge in venture was _access to information._ Who knew about the company first. Who had the network to get the intro. Who saw the round before it was a round.

That moat is draining fast.

When everyone runs a deep data set, nobody has one. When 15 million companies are tracked by a dozen platforms, "I found it early" stops being a flex — it's table stakes. The same signal that gives you a 14-month head start gives every other fund on the same software the identical head start.

This is the part the Tier-1 firms should be sweating, not the emerging managers.

The big brands built their dominance on being _gatherers_ — sit still, let the best founders apply, let the referrals roll in. That worked when prestige was the scarce resource. But AI doesn't care about your logo. It surfaces the founder in Tulsa nobody flew out to meet. It democratizes the one thing that used to be locked behind a Sand Hill address: knowing the company exists.

Information was the moat. AI just filled in the moat and paved a parking lot on top.

## **What It Can't Eat**

So far this reads bleak. Now the turn.

**AI commoditizes the search. It does not commoditize the conviction.**

Sourcing tells you a company exists. It cannot tell you to wire $2 million into a 25-year-old with a demo, a dream, and a competitor that just raised from a16z. That's not a data problem. That's a _nerve_ problem.

Four things the model can't do, and probably won't:

**It can't see what isn't public.** 

Every model — Motherbrain included — eats the same exhaust: LinkedIn, app store ranks, funding data, the public scrape. That's the floor, not the edge. The signal that actually moves a decision lives where no crawler can reach — the real retention curve behind the vanity chart, the customer who tells you off the record that they'd riot if the product disappeared, the back-channel reference that never gets indexed, the number the founder only says out loud on the third call. Proprietary data isn't _found._ It's earned — relationship by relationship, call by call. The machine gets the internet. You get the truth founders only tell people they trust. Public data is a commodity. Private data is the moat.

**It can't have conviction.** 

A score is not a decision. When the algorithm spits out a 73 and the founder makes the hair on your neck stand up, the machine has no opinion about which one to trust. Judgment under uncertainty — with real money, real reputation, and no clean answer — is the entire job once the busywork is gone.

**It can't get the allocation.** 

The best deals are oversubscribed. Getting in isn't an information game, it's a _relationship _game — years of trust, a reputation for being helpful when it didn't pay, a founder who picks your check over a bigger one because you took their 11pm call. No agent earns that.

**It can't be wrong in public.** 

Every great venture bet looks stupid at the moment it's made. AI is trained on consensus — on what _already worked._ It pattern-matches to the last winner. But the returns live in the bets that don't pattern-match yet. The non-consensus, look-foolish-now, prove-it-later swing. The machine is structurally built to talk you _out_ of those.

The model optimizes for the defensible no. Venture is paid for the indefensible yes.

## **The 2% Game Gets Automated. The 20% Game Doesn't.**

I've written before about venture's slow drift from a 20% game (earn your carry by picking winners) to a 2% game (collect your management fee, stay comfortable). AI just drew that line in permanent marker.

Everything on the 2% side — the headcount, the process, the deck-reading theater that justified the fee — that's the part getting automated to zero. If your value to your LPs was "we have a big team that looks at a lot of deals," a $40/month subscription now does that.

Everything on the 20% side — taste, conviction, access, the stomach to be early and alone — that's the part that just became _the entire value proposition._

For emerging managers and angels, this is the best news in a decade. The hunter's edge was always judgment plus hustle, never headcount. AI hands you the headcount for free. Now you compete on the only axis that ever mattered.

For LPs: stop paying 2% for a process a machine runs better. Start underwriting the human for the only thing the human still does — pick, and have the spine to be early. A fund that can't articulate an edge beyond "our sourcing engine" is selling you software with a carry attached.

## **The Bottom Line**

Will AI eat the VC?

It already ate the analyst. It's halfway through the gatherer. And it's quietly exposing every "investor" who was really just a well-dressed search function.

But the picker? The hunter? The one with conviction, access, and the nerve to look wrong on the way to being right?

AI doesn't replace that investor. It deletes everyone hiding behind busywork and leaves that investor standing alone — with better tools and fewer places to hide.

The machine made information free. Now venture is finally, brutally, a judgment business.

Which is what it should have been the whole time.

------------------------------------------------------------

Jeff Dean, Google’s chief scientist, left Google with a group of other senior colleagues to start a blue sky research lab. He’d been at Google since 1999. Demis Hassabis, co-founder of Deepmind and currently CEO, will step up/down/aside to be chairman.

👋 Hey there, I’m Lenny. Each week, I share deeply researched product, growth, and career advice. For more: Lenny’s Podcast [ https://substack.com/redirect/96fb7e95-76b5-44d2-9d34-00ba7d0d967c?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] | Lennybot [ https://substack.com/redirect/d62650ac-ef44-4b53-9c49-6e24e1499097?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] | How I AI [ https://substack.com/redirect/e1c0516d-8058-4bda-99ce-a6e748f4b63b?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] | Become an AI-Native Builder [ https://substack.com/redirect/1042edba-bc12-4a3c-9b2c-701a32e89f33?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and other favorite AI/PM courses [ https://substack.com/redirect/0b560e61-5fd8-45b7-8242-36959dd28646?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]

Learn more [ https://substack.com/redirect/a2d5f3e2-5012-44c9-8882-27397e216ba6?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
Kristen does such an incredible job of introducing this piece that I’ll just skip my regular intro and jump right into it.
Kristen Lowe is an executive ghostwriter and narrative strategist, and the incoming Director of Founder & Editorial Communications at Scribe [ https://substack.com/redirect/a52235d0-3db7-4315-8d2a-c10e83554823?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ]. Previously the Director of Operations at Hinge, she has built founder communication platforms across LinkedIn, Substack, X, and keynote stages, and written for leaders in every format from essays to TED Talks. You can find more of her work on AI, careers, and storytelling on Substack [ https://substack.com/redirect/93e8e006-442c-41c6-ae16-9152a1d4ee69?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ] and TikTok [ https://substack.com/redirect/d63283e3-d723-42a9-a82e-f35844c77a57?j=eyJ1IjoiMmU2aDEifQ.VGKrlpe010xZBcMagL3trNwkDdJUfw_qmH45MbfoDHA ].
It’s never been easier to start a company. It’s also never been harder to get someone to care that you did. Anyone can now go from idea to business in less time than it takes to hire a single engineer. But the same tools that make building simple make standing out a challenge.
As channels like X and LinkedIn flood with soulless AI slop, startups are having to work harder to grab people’s already fractured attention amid all the noise. But this moment presents an opportunity for founders who can say something honest and connective by “going direct”—or what I call founder-led communication. Today, a solid founder-led communications strategy is one of the lowest-cost, highest-leverage tools at your disposal to get people’s attention.
Most founders seem to know this. When I started writing for founders as an executive ghostwriter and comms strategist, the biggest surprise was the constant stream of inbound clients at all stages who thought they “should” be building a public platform but didn’t know how to start. I’d assumed people would want ghostwriting help because they just hated writing, but the number one reason founders reached out for help was “I have no idea what to say.”
There’s a discouraging misconception that for comms to be impactful, you have to be vulnerable, contrarian, or profoundly entertaining in every message you put out there. I hear from founders all the time who are daunted by that expectation. But in my experience, the only thing most people need to build a credible comms strategy is an answer to the question “Why did I start this company?”
This answer is usually the most narratively powerful idea to share about your business. Starting a company is a life-altering pursuit with a famously high failure rate. Whatever reason sent you down that path, it was once compelling enough to rearrange your whole life around and recruit others to do the same. Founder communications work because people care about and root for other humans, not entities or widgets.
More importantly, if you’re not excited about the story of why you started this company, you should probably look for a different line of work. As more people stray from traditional career ladders and as entrepreneurship becomes more popular, there will be a wave of founders who start companies simply because they can, or because it looks like a fast track to a lot of money. People can tell when you’re in it for the wrong reasons—which includes no reason at all. There’s no comms strategy for that. But for everyone else: if your reason was convincing enough for you, it’s convincing enough to make other people care too.
Once you know your “why,” this guide will help you figure out the right strategic communications choices for your business, so all you have to do is start writing and hit post.
The three founder archetypes
While every founder’s “why” is unique, they almost always fall into one of three categories, each mapping to a founder archetype that can help you define your comms strategy:
The “Problem” founder: The person who started a company to solve their own problem
The “Insight” founder: The person who started a company to solve a problem only they saw
The “Vision” founder: The person who started a company because they imagined a better world
Lumping yourself into an archetype might seem like a counterintuitive way to build distinctive founder content, but the ways people connect with founders map to these three relationships: I identify with you, I trust you, I’d follow you. A unique story makes your content interesting, but your archetype determines which feeling it evokes in your audience, and cultivating the right one for your business requires different strategic choices.
Your founder archetype will guide you to the decisions that matter for a comms strategy:
Goal: What specifically your content strategy is meant to achieve
Voice: How you should sound
Messaging pillars: What you should talk about
Success conditions: How you’ll know if it’s working
What your founder archetype will not tell you are answers to questions like “How often should I post?” Founder comms are like workout routines: the best one is the one you can commit to. Regardless of your archetype, committing to any channel and cadence that works for you beats agonizing over the perfect one. And everything else you might be worried about—audience segmentation, attribution, earned vs. organic media balance—is secondary. You can tackle that once you have a substantial body of content to optimize around.
Archetype 1: The “Problem” founder
The Problem founder is someone who started their business to solve a problem that was personally tormenting them. Think Sara Blakely, who hated how pantyhose looked under her pants, so she cut the feet off them and founded Spanx, or Tobi Lütke, who tried to sell snowboards and got so frustrated with the existing e-commerce programs that he decided it would be easier to build Shopify instead.
What makes these founders compelling is that they understand the customer better than anyone else could, because they are the customer. When you’re solving a problem because it caused you so much pain that you restructured your life around fixing it, you have a unique power to make your customer feel seen and understood. You get to say that you’re working for “us,” not for “them,” and your success becomes “our success.” That narrative is a powerful tool for building affiliation and brand loyalty. The Problem founder has a singular ability to identify as a customer first and business owner second, which should anchor their entire comms strategy.
